```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 4.6, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%",
                      dev = if (requireNamespace("svglite", quietly = TRUE)) "svglite" else
                        if (isTRUE(capabilities("cairo"))) "svg" else "png")
library(Rcausality)
# Long-running results (benchmarks, method comparisons) are precomputed and
# shipped in vignettes/precomputed/ so that the vignette builds in about a
# minute; the code shown is exactly the code that produced them.
# Sys.setenv(RCAUSALITY_RECOMPUTE = "true") recomputes everything.
.pre <- function(name, expr) {
  f <- file.path("precomputed", paste0(name, ".rds"))
  if (file.exists(f) && !identical(Sys.getenv("RCAUSALITY_RECOMPUTE"), "true")) return(readRDS(f))
  v <- expr
  dir.create("precomputed", showWarnings = FALSE)
  saveRDS(v, f, compress = "xz")
  v
}
```

# What the package does

`Rcausality` detects **directed (causal) relations between time series**.
Two traditions meet here:

* the **predictive** notion of Granger (1969): $x$ causes $y$ if the past
  of $x$ helps to predict $y$ beyond what the past of $y$ already tells
  (linear Granger causality, Bayesian Granger causality, conditional mutual
  information, transfer entropy, partial information decomposition, the
  Markov-chain approach, the degrees-of-freedom / conditional-variance
  method);
* the **dynamical-systems** notion built on the embedding theorem of
  Takens (1981) and the reconstruction of a driver from the driven
  system:
  convergent cross mapping, dimensional causality, the complexity-based
  CCDH, recurrence-plot criteria and correlation-dimension relations.

All methods are called through **one function**, `rcausality()`, and return
**one kind of object**, `causres`, that prints, summarises, plots and
compares the same way. Every method reports, per ordered pair of series,
a test statistic, a p-value and/or a Bayes factor, an effect size and a
decision, and classifies each unordered pair into one of five cases:

| class | meaning |
|---|---|
| `x_to_y` | $x$ drives $y$ |
| `y_to_x` | $y$ drives $x$ |
| `bidirectional` | mutual coupling |
| `common_cause` | no directed link, but a hidden common driver (only for methods able to detect it) |
| `independent` | no relation found |

This vignette shows the everyday use. The companion vignette
*The methods, paper by paper* (`vignette("methods", package = "Rcausality")`)
explains every method, gives the full references and reproduces results
of the papers they come from.

# A first analysis

## Simulated data with a known answer

The package ships simulators whose causal structure is known, so every
step can be checked. `sim_var()` draws a bivariate VAR(1) process in which
`x` drives `y` with one lag:

$$x_t = 0.5\,x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_{x,t}, \qquad
  y_t = 0.5\,y_{t-1} + 0.4\,x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_{y,t}.$$

```{r data, fig.height = 3.8, fig.cap = "Two simulated AR(1) series; x drives y with one lag (sim_var, scenario x_to_y)."}
d <- sim_var(400, "x_to_y", seed = 1)
plot_series(d, n_last = 200, main = "sim_var(400, 'x_to_y')")
```

## Granger causality in one call

```{r granger}
r <- rcausality(d)          # Granger causality (F-test); lag order chosen by BIC
r
```

How to read the output:

* **one row per directed test** (`y -> x` and `x -> y`): `lag` is the
  VAR order selected by the information criterion, `F` the test statistic
  with its degrees of freedom, `p` the raw and `p.adj` the Holm-adjusted
  p-value, `BF10` the BIC-approximated Bayes factor for the link and
  `P.post` the posterior probability of the link given a 50 % prior;
* `sig` is the decision (`*` codes as in `summary.lm`);
* the **classification** block reads the two directions together.

`summary()` gives the compact version and the object can be turned into a
data frame or a matrix:

```{r summary}
summary(r)
as.data.frame(r)[, c("cause", "effect", "lag", "statistic", "p_adj", "effect_size", "r2_gain", "significant")]
as.matrix(r, "p_adj")      # cause (rows) -> effect (columns)
```

The effect size is Geweke's (1982) measure $\log(RSS_r / RSS_u)$ and the
$R^2$ gain of adding the cause's lags; `sign` gives the sign of the summed
coefficients of the cause.

# Several series

## All ordered pairs of a data frame

A data frame with more columns is analysed for every ordered pair. For a
random sparse VAR network the true adjacency matrix is attached to the
simulated data:

```{r network-data, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "A four-variable VAR network (sim_var with n_series = 4)."}
net <- sim_var(500, n_series = 4, seed = 42)
attr(net, "adjacency")         # TRUE where row -> column in the simulation
plot_series(net, n_last = 150)
```

```{r network}
rn <- rcausality(net)
rn$classes[, c("var1", "var2", "relation", "p_adj_12", "p_adj_21")]
```

## Plots: network, causal matrix, lag scan

`plot()` draws the causal network (edge width ~ evidence, label = lag,
colour = sign of the net effect), the causal matrix (cause rows -> effect
columns, significant links starred), the statistic of every pair against
the candidate lag, and the joint delay embedding of the strongest pair;
`type = "all"` puts the four together.

```{r plots, dev = "png", dpi = 110, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 8.5, fig.cap = "plot(rn, 'all'): causal network, causal matrix, lag scan and joint embedding."}
plot(rn, "all")
```

The lag scan is useful when the coupling delay is unknown: the selected
lag is marked by an open circle, significant pairs are drawn with solid
lines.

```{r lags, fig.height = 4.2, fig.cap = "Lag scan: F statistic of every directed pair against the candidate lag."}
plot(rn, "lags")
```

## Blocks of series (MIMO) and conditioning

Two blocks of series (`x` = candidate causes, `y` = candidate effects) are
tested block-wise, in both directions by default or only forward:

```{r blocks}
rcausality(net[, 1:2], net[, 3:4], directions = "forward")$pairs[, c("cause", "effect", "lag", "p_adj", "significant")]
```

With several series an apparent link can be mediated by a third one
(`v1 -> v2 -> v3` looks like `v1 -> v3` pairwise). `conditional = TRUE`
conditions every test on the remaining series (conditional Granger
causality), which keeps only direct links:

```{r conditional}
rcausality(net, conditional = TRUE)$classes[, c("var1", "var2", "relation")]
```

# Non-linear coupling: model-free methods

Linear Granger causality tests a linear regression and can miss
non-linear coupling. `sim_logistic()` couples two logistic maps,
$x_{t+1} = r x_t (1 - x_t)$, with $x$ driving $y$ through a non-linear
term. The time series look like noise, but the delay embedding reveals the
deterministic structure.

```{r logistic, fig.height = 3.8, fig.cap = "Coupled logistic maps (x drives y)."}
lg <- sim_logistic(500, "x_to_y", seed = 2)
plot_series(lg, n_last = 120)
```

```{r embedding, dev = "png", dpi = 110, fig.height = 4.2, fig.cap = "Delay embeddings: the driver x on its own (left) and the joint state (x[t-1], y[t], x[t]) (right)."}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2)); plot_embedding(lg$x, m = 2); plot_embedding(lg$x, lg$y); par(op)
```

`method = "cmi"` estimates the conditional mutual information
$I(x_{t-\text{lag}};\, y_t \mid y_{t-1}, \dots)$ with the Frenzel-Pompe
(2007) k-nearest-neighbour estimator and tests it with Runge's (2018)
local-permutation null; `method = "te"` is the binned transfer entropy of
Schreiber (2000); `method = "ccm"` is Sugihara et al.'s (2012) convergent
cross mapping. The verdicts of several methods can be compared in one
call:

```{r compare, eval = FALSE}
cm <- compare_methods(lg, methods = c("granger", "cmi", "te", "ccm"), seed = 1)
cm
plot(cm)
```

```{r compare-run, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.2, fig.cap = "compare_methods(): verdict of every method per pair with the majority consensus."}
cm <- .pre("compare", compare_methods(lg, methods = c("granger", "cmi", "te", "ccm"), seed = 1))
cm
plot(cm)
```

Granger misses the non-linear link here while the three model-free
methods find it. The CCM result can be inspected through the cross-map
skill against the library size (`plot(r, "lags")` for a `ccm` result):

```{r ccm, fig.height = 4.2, fig.cap = "Convergent cross mapping: the skill of predicting x from the embedding of y rises with the library size (y 'knows' x because x drives it)."}
rc <- rcausality(lg, method = "ccm", seed = 1)
plot(rc, "lags")
```

# Hidden common drivers

Two series can be correlated without either driving the other, because
a third, unobserved process drives both. Zlatniczki et al. (2021) show
that the contemporaneous dependence of $x_t$ and $y_t$ *given both pasts*
reveals such a common driver when no lagged dependence exists;
`method = "cmi_lag"` implements this and returns the `common_cause` class.

```{r common, eval = FALSE}
set.seed(5); n <- 400
e1 <- rnorm(n); e2 <- 0.8 * e1 + 0.6 * rnorm(n)        # shared innovation = hidden common driver
cc <- data.frame(x = as.numeric(stats::filter(e1, 0.5, "recursive")),
                 y = as.numeric(stats::filter(e2, 0.5, "recursive")))
rcc <- rcausality(cc, method = "cmi_lag", seed = 1)
rcc
```

```{r common-run, echo = FALSE}
set.seed(5); n <- 400
e1 <- rnorm(n); e2 <- 0.8 * e1 + 0.6 * rnorm(n)
cc <- data.frame(x = as.numeric(stats::filter(e1, 0.5, "recursive")),
                 y = as.numeric(stats::filter(e2, 0.5, "recursive")))
rcc <- .pre("common", rcausality(cc, method = "cmi_lag", seed = 1))
rcc
```

The `instant` table holds the contemporaneous test; the network plot
draws a dashed orange edge for common-driver evidence:

```{r common-plot, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Common driver: no directed link, but contemporaneous dependence given both pasts."}
plot(rcc, "both")
```

# Comparative analyses

## Several data sets, several methods

A quick way to see where methods agree is to run `compare_methods()` on
data sets with different kinds of coupling. Here: a linear VAR link, a
non-linear logistic link and the common-driver pair above.

```{r compare-table, eval = FALSE}
sets <- list(VAR = sim_var(400, "x_to_y", seed = 1), logistic = lg, common_driver = cc)
meths <- c("granger", "cmi", "cmi_lag", "te")
tab <- t(sapply(sets, function(s) compare_methods(s, methods = meths, seed = 1, lag = 1)$table[1, meths]))
tab <- as.data.frame(tab); tab$truth <- c("x_to_y", "x_to_y", "common_cause"); tab
```

```{r compare-table-run, echo = FALSE}
tab <- .pre("compare-table", {
  sets <- list(VAR = sim_var(400, "x_to_y", seed = 1), logistic = lg, common_driver = cc)
  meths <- c("granger", "cmi", "cmi_lag", "te")
  tab <- t(sapply(sets, function(s) compare_methods(s, methods = meths, seed = 1, lag = 1)$table[1, meths]))
  tab <- as.data.frame(tab); tab$truth <- c("x_to_y", "x_to_y", "common_cause"); tab
})
tab
```

(`lag = 1` fixes the coupling lag, which is known here, and saves the lag
search.) Only `cmi_lag` can name the common driver; the others report
(correctly) that neither series Granger-causes the other, which the
classification calls `independent`.

## Benchmark with known truth

`benchmark_methods()` simulates every scenario of a simulator several
times, runs the methods and scores the class against the truth. Small
sizes are used here to keep the vignette quick; in practice use more
replications.

```{r benchmark, eval = FALSE}
bm <- benchmark_methods(methods = c("granger", "cmi", "te"), scenarios = c("x_to_y", "bidirectional", "independent"),
                        simulator = sim_var, n = 300, reps = 2, seed = 1, args = list(cmi = list(lag = 1)))
bm
plot(bm)
```

```{r benchmark-run, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "benchmark_methods(): accuracy per scenario on linear VAR data."}
bm <- .pre("benchmark", benchmark_methods(methods = c("granger", "cmi", "te"), scenarios = c("x_to_y", "bidirectional", "independent"),
                        simulator = sim_var, n = 300, reps = 2, seed = 1, args = list(cmi = list(lag = 1))))
bm$simulator <- "sim_var"
bm
plot(bm)
```

The same on coupled logistic maps, where the linear test is at a
disadvantage:

```{r benchmark2, eval = FALSE}
bm2 <- benchmark_methods(methods = c("granger", "cmi", "te", "ccm"), scenarios = c("x_to_y", "independent"),
                         simulator = sim_logistic, n = 300, reps = 2, seed = 1, args = list(cmi = list(lag = 1)))
plot(bm2)
```

```{r benchmark2-run, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Accuracy per scenario on coupled logistic maps."}
bm2 <- .pre("benchmark2", benchmark_methods(methods = c("granger", "cmi", "te", "ccm"), scenarios = c("x_to_y", "independent"),
                         simulator = sim_logistic, n = 300, reps = 2, seed = 1, args = list(cmi = list(lag = 1))))
bm2$simulator <- "sim_logistic"
plot(bm2)
```

`bm$confusion` holds the confusion matrix of every method and `bm$time`
the mean seconds per run, which matters when choosing a method for long
series.

# Bayesian variants of the methods

Every method has a Bayesian variant, switched on with `bayes = TRUE`; its
priors, iterations and decision rule are collected in `bayes_control()`.
The result is the same `causres` object, with `bf10` (Bayes factor),
`post_prob` (posterior probability of the link) and `evidence` filled for
every directed test, the details per link in `$bayes`, and a link declared
when $BF_{10}$ exceeds `bf_threshold` (or, with
`decision = "posterior"`, when the posterior exceeds `prob_threshold`).

## Granger causality as a Bayesian regression

The effect is regressed on its own past, the controls and the cause's
past. With the default `prior = "spike_slab"` every cause lag has a
point-mass spike at zero and a normal slab of scale `scale` $\times\sigma$
(stochastic-search variable selection, George and McCulloch 1993); the
lag subsets are enumerated exactly, so the posterior inclusion probability
of every lag and the Bayes factor of "at least one lag" against "none" are
exact, and `chains` $\times$ `n_iter` posterior draws (after `burnin`,
every `thin`-th kept) give credible intervals of the coefficients and of
Geweke's measure $\log(1 + \text{explained}/\sigma^2)$, with the effective
sample size and the Gelman-Rubin $\hat R$ of the measure across the chains
(values close to 1: the chains agree). With more than 12 lags the
indicators are Gibbs-sampled instead of enumerated.

```{r bayes}
bc <- bayes_control(prior = "spike_slab", scale = 1, inclusion_prob = 0.5, n_iter = 1000, chains = 2, credible = 0.95)
rb <- rcausality(d, bayes = TRUE, control = bc, seed = 1)
rb
rb$bayes_fits[["x -> y"]]
```

`prior = "normal"` compares the whole block of cause lags against none,
and `"g"`, `"hyper_g"`, `"bic"` are the closed-form Bayes factors:

```{r bayes-priors}
sapply(c("spike_slab", "normal", "g", "hyper_g", "bic"), function(pr)
  rcausality(d, bayes = TRUE, control = bayes_control(prior = pr, n_iter = 200, chains = 1))$pairs$bf10)
```

## The surrogate methods: a Bayesian surrogate test

The model-free methods compare a statistic with surrogate / permutation
draws. Their Bayesian variant keeps the surrogates as the null model
(`null_model = "kde"` or `"normal"`) and puts a prior on the effect: a
half-Cauchy (default), half-normal, Cauchy or normal distribution of scale
`scale` surrogate standard deviations (`effect_prior`). The Bayes factor
$f_1(T)/f_0(T)$ is integrated over the prior (`n_draws`), and the
posterior of the effect is reported with a credible interval.

```{r bayes2}
rc <- rcausality(lg, method = "cmi", lag = 1, bayes = TRUE, seed = 1,
                 control = bayes_control(effect_prior = "half_cauchy", scale = 1, null_model = "kde", n_draws = 4000))
rc$bayes
surrogate_bf(0.23, rnorm(200, 0, 0.02))     # the generic test on its own
```

The posterior-based methods take a prior over the five causal cases
(`case_prior`), the Markov-chain approach combines the Bayes factors of
its six tests through the decision table, and `plot(r, "posterior")`
shows the posterior probabilities and effect intervals:

```{r bayes-plot, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "plot(rb, 'posterior'): posterior probability of every directed link with its Bayes factor, and the credible interval of Geweke's measure."}
rcausality(sim_logistic_bdc(800, "x_to_y", seed = 1), method = "dc", bayes = TRUE,
           control = bayes_control(case_prior = c(1, 1, 1, 4, 4)))$pairs[, c("cause", "effect", "post_prob", "bf10")]
plot(rb, "posterior")
```

# Causality-informed forecasting

The detected links define a **restricted VAR**: every series is regressed
on its own lags and on the lags of its significant causes only.
`predict()` compares this model with the own-lags model by rolling
one-step forecasts on the last 20 % of the sample, and forecasts `h`
steps ahead with intervals from the multi-step MSE recursion (Luetkepohl,
2005):

```{r forecast, fig.height = 7, fig.cap = "predict(): hold-out one-step predictions of the own-lags model (dashed) and the causal model (blue), and the h-step forecasts with 95 % intervals."}
fc <- predict(rn, h = 8)
fc
plot(fc, n_last = 80)
```

The driven series gain from their causes; the undriven ones are forecast
by their own lags alone (0 % change), as they should be.

# Practical matters

## Speed and several cores

The kNN and surrogate-based methods cost $O(n^2)$ per permutation. A C++
back-end keeps them fast for series of a few thousand points, and `cores`
distributes the work over several CPU cores: the series pairs when there
are at least as many pairs as cores, otherwise the permutations or
surrogates of every test; `bayes_granger()` runs its chains in parallel,
`benchmark_methods()` its replications. Every unit of work draws from its
own L'Ecuyer-CMRG random stream, so **the results do not depend on the
number of cores**: for a given `seed`, `cores = 1` and `cores = 8` give the
same p-values, Bayes factors and verdicts to the last digit, and the
session's generator is left where a serial call leaves it. Forked workers
are used on Linux and macOS, a socket cluster (started for the call and closed at its end) on
Windows, where the package must be installed; a cluster object from
`parallel::makeCluster()` is accepted too, and `options(Rcausality.cores =)`
sets the default for the session (`?Rcausality-parallel`).

```{r cores, eval = FALSE}
rcausality(net, method = "cmi", cores = 4, seed = 1)
rcausality(net, method = "cmi", cores = "auto", seed = 1)   # all physical cores but one
options(Rcausality.cores = 4)                               # for every call of the session
```

```{r cores-check, echo = TRUE}
r1 <- rcausality(lg, method = "te", seed = 1, cores = 1)
r2 <- rcausality(lg, method = "te", seed = 1, cores = 2)
identical(r1$pairs, r2$pairs)
```

## Your own data

Numeric columns of a data frame are the series. `prep_series()`
differences, standardises and imputes; stationarity matters for the
regression-based methods, while the embedding-based ones need long, low-
noise series.

```{r own, eval = FALSE}
my <- read.csv("series.csv")
my <- prep_series(my, diff = 1)          # first differences, linear interpolation of NAs
plot_series(my)
res <- rcausality(my, method = "cmi", cores = "auto", seed = 1)
res; plot(res, "all")
compare_methods(my, methods = c("granger", "cmi", "te"), seed = 1)
```

## Which method?

* Linear, stochastic series: `"granger"` / `"bayes_granger"`, with
  `conditional = TRUE` for several series.
* Non-linear stochastic coupling: `"cmi"`, `"te"`, `"pid"`; `"cmi_lag"`
  when a hidden common driver is suspected; `"markov"` for the
  Markov-property reading.
* Deterministic (chaotic) systems observed with little noise: `"dc"`,
  `"ccdh"`, `"ccm"`, `"hirata"`, `"cd"`; `"df"` for the
  degrees-of-freedom reading of either kind of system.
* Many autocorrelated candidates: `"pcmci"` (needs the Python package
  tigramite) or conditional Granger / CMI.
